introduction-the-pending-pod-problem.core: When Kubernetes can't schedule a pod because no node has enough free CPU, memory or the right features, the pod stays Pending. Node autoscalers watch for pending pods and add capacity, and remove under-used nodes later. How they choose and remove nodes decides speed, cost and stability.

first_principles.problem: Traffic spikes leave pods Pending for minutes while users see errors.

analogy.title: A restaurant adding tables when guests queue
analogy.story: How fast and how smartly you add tables decides wait times and wasted space.
analogy.breaks: Restaurants can seat guests anywhere; pods have constraints (zones, GPUs, taints).

check.q: What triggers a node autoscaler to add capacity?
check.a: Pods that are Pending because no existing node can satisfy their requests or constraints.

cluster-autoscaler-cas-the-asg-manager.core: Cluster Autoscaler works through node groups (Auto Scaling groups). It simulates whether adding a node from an existing group would schedule pending pods, then bumps that ASG's desired count, and scales down nodes whose pods can move elsewhere. It's limited to pre-defined instance types per group and is relatively slow.

first_principles.problem: A cluster needs a dozen node groups to cover different instance types, and scaling takes minutes.
truths: Simulation picks a group, not an instance type.
derivation: CAS picks a group via **expanders** (least-waste, priority).
Use **one AZ per group** for zonal volumes.

analogy.title: Ordering from a fixed catalogue
analogy.story: You can only buy the pre-packaged bundles, even if you need something slightly different.
analogy.breaks: Catalogues ship quickly; ASG scale-up involves extra API hops.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Picks the group with least idle resources.

check.q: Why do clusters using CAS often have many node groups?
check.a: Each ASG has fixed instance types, so different shapes, zones or purchase options need separate groups.

karpenter-just-in-time-provisioning.core: Karpenter watches pending pods and launches EC2 instances directly through the EC2 Fleet API, choosing the best-fit instance type from a broad set defined in NodePools (constraints like families, sizes, architecture, Spot/On-Demand, zones). No node groups are needed, and nodes typically join in under a minute.

first_principles.problem: CAS can only pick from preset groups and scales slowly.
truths: Pods' combined requests define the ideal node.
EC2 offers hundreds of instance types.
Direct API calls are faster than ASG indirection.
derivation: Karpenter **batches pending pods** and picks types.

analogy.title: A tailor making a suit on demand
analogy.story: Instead of picking off the rack, it cuts exactly what fits.
analogy.breaks: Tailors take weeks; Karpenter takes seconds, but it still depends on EC2 capacity.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Best-fit, diversified nodes in under a minute.

check.q: What replaces node groups in Karpenter?
check.a: NodePools (with EC2NodeClasses) defining constraints, from which Karpenter picks instance types.

bin-packing-the-game-of-tetris.core: Bin packing fits pods onto as few nodes as possible to minimise waste. Karpenter considers pending pods' combined requests and picks instance types that fit them tightly; consolidation later repacks running pods onto fewer or cheaper nodes. Accurate resource requests are essential, since bad requests make good packing impossible.

first_principles.problem: Nodes average 30% utilisation because pods request far more than they use.
truths: Schedulers pack by requests, not usage.
Larger nodes pack better but increase blast radius.
derivation: Let Karpenter **choose sizes** to fit batches.

analogy.title: Playing Tetris with pods
analogy.story: Fitting pieces tightly clears lines and saves space; odd shapes leave holes.
analogy.breaks: Tetris pieces are fixed; pod requests can (and should) be tuned.

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Packing quality depends on honest requests.

check.q: Why do inflated pod requests hurt bin packing?
check.a: The scheduler reserves requested capacity, so nodes look full while actually idle.

disruption-consolidation-cleaning-up.core: Karpenter's disruption controller removes or replaces nodes when they're empty, underutilised (consolidation into fewer or cheaper nodes), expired (max node lifetime for patching) or drifted from the NodePool/NodeClass spec. It respects PodDisruptionBudgets and disruption budgets to limit how many nodes churn at once.

first_principles.problem: Nodes launched for a spike linger at 10% usage for days, and old AMIs never get replaced.
truths: Long-lived nodes accumulate drift and vulnerabilities.

analogy.title: A cleaning crew that merges half-empty storage rooms
analogy.story: They move items into fewer rooms and close the empties, but never during business-critical hours.
analogy.breaks: Moving boxes is harmless; evicting pods restarts them, so apps must tolerate it.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Cleanup outside business hours; nodes rotated monthly.

code.text:
disruption:
  consolidationPolicy: WhenEmptyOrUnderutilized
  consolidateAfter: 5m
  budgets:
    - nodes: "10%"
    - nodes: "0"
      schedule: "0 9 * * mon-fri"
      duration: 8h
template:
  spec:
    expireAfter: 720h

check.a: A node no longer matches its NodePool/EC2NodeClass spec (e.g. new AMI), so it's replaced.

head-to-head-comparison-when-to-use-each.core: Karpenter is faster, more flexible (any instance type, no node groups), packs and consolidates better and simplifies Spot diversification; it's the default choice on EKS today. Cluster Autoscaler is cloud-agnostic, mature, and fits environments that must stay on ASGs or managed node groups with fixed shapes. Some clusters run both during migration.

first_principles.problem: A team must choose an autoscaler for a new EKS platform.
derivation: **Karpenter** for EKS, varied workloads, Spot, cost focus.
**CAS** for multi-cloud parity or strict ASG requirements.
Run Karpenter controller on **Fargate or a small fixed node group**.

analogy.title: A ride-hailing app versus a fixed bus timetable
analogy.story: Ride-hailing sends the right car when needed; buses are predictable but rigid.
analogy.breaks: Buses work everywhere; Karpenter's AWS provider is the most mature, others less so.

example.title: Migration plan
flow: Install Karpenter on a small managed node group

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Faster scaling, ~20–30% lower compute cost typical.

example.outcome: the right autoscaler for the platform.

check.q: Where should the Karpenter controller run?
check.a: On capacity it doesn't manage itself, such as Fargate or a small fixed managed node group.
